summary:
The United Arab Emirates subjects trans travellers to gender-document screening at the border. In 2025 two foreign trans women were held for hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched the female sex recorded in their passports, mocked by staff, and denied entry with their passports confiscated.

Refusals of entry on identity grounds are documented across a decade. In August 2016 the trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was denied entry and detained for five hours at Dubai International Airport because authorities did not recognise her gender as legitimate, and her passport was confiscated. In March 2022 the Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, runner-up in the 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe contest, was stopped at Dubai immigration, interrogated for nine hours and deported to Thailand ahead of her Expo 2020 appearance; her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

The legal framework underpinning these encounters explicitly acknowledges and penalises nonconformity with traditional gender roles, and transgender expression or an unconventional appearance frequently lead to arrest, confinement or expulsion.

Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Article 409(1)(b) of the Federal Crimes and Penalties Law (2021), which carries a minimum of six months' imprisonment with no maximum prescribed. Outright International's UAE overview, updated in March 2026, describes the federal criminal code enacted in early 2022 as criminalising consensual same-sex relations with up to six months' imprisonment, with charges requiring a complaint basis.

Article 412(2) provides that men who disguise themselves as women to enter a women-only space may be imprisoned for up to one year and fined up to AED 10,000. That provision replaced a broader previous ban on clothing deemed inappropriate for one's sex.

No legal gender recognition is available in the United Arab Emirates, and sex reassignment surgery is severely restricted to limited, highly state-regulated circumstances. No UAE law or policy prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and gay conversion practices are neither prohibited nor discouraged by any law or regulation.

Detention conditions carry documented risks for gender-nonconforming people. Detainees have been held in cells designated for 'effeminate' people, and involuntary medical and psychological treatments, including hormonal therapies and detention for forced psychological treatment, have occurred in connection with suspected or established same-sex sexual conduct. Reports of mistreatment in detention include beatings and forced rectal examinations amounting to torture.

A Brazilian trans woman held in UAE custody from September 2022, after being arrested for refusing a police-requested toxicology test, accused the consulate of negligence. Her case is a documented instance of a trans foreigner in prolonged UAE custody.

Support infrastructure available to a visitor in difficulty is absent. No LGBTQI+ support or advocacy organisations operate openly anywhere in the country, LGBTI organisations cannot register, the United Arab Emirates does not recognise same-sex marriage, and in Dubai a nightclub that sponsored a night for the LGBTQ community was shut down by the government.
tangentialFactors:
Censorship extends to trans representation. The country's sole internet provider blocks sites on dating, marriage and LGBTQ issues and reportedly any site containing the word 'gay' or 'sex'. The Media Regulatory Office banned Pixar's Lightyear in June 2022 over a same-sex relationship and banned Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse in June 2023 over a scene showing a 'Protect Trans Lives' transgender flag; the Arabic children's comic Majid came under investigation in 2022, and in June 2023 Amazon blocked 150 search terms including 'lgbtq' and 'pride' on its UAE site under threat of penalties.

Official rhetoric is openly hostile. Officials have publicly declared there is 'no room for homosexual and queer acts in the UAE', and social attitudes toward varied gender expression are described as combining with the likelihood of state repression to prevent community organising and education.

Comparative indices place the country low but not at the bottom: it ranked 85th with a score of 37 on PlanetRomeo's 2015 Gay Happiness Index. Entertainment industry pushback has also been recorded, with the band Steps refusing a Dubai show in June 2023 over a contract clause barring disclosure of their sexuality.
localsOnly:
Charges under Article 409(1)(b) may be brought only on a complaint by the spouse or guardian of the complainant, who may withdraw it at any time. Because civil guardianship ends at age 18, no eligible complainant exists for consensual conduct between adult men, so federal prosecution is not possible in that case. For conduct between women, an unmarried Muslim woman's father or male relative may qualify as guardian under the Islamic wali concept and a married woman's husband as spouse, so prosecution remains possible where such a complainant exists.

Enforcement against gender expression is documented. In December 2013 two Brazilian transgender women who called police about prejudice they had witnessed in a nightclub were themselves arrested for 'imitating women', held until March 2014, fined AED 10,000 and ordered deported.

Police raids and arrests for same-sex conduct and cross-dressing include the 2005 Abu Dhabi desert resort raid on 26 young men accused of cross-dressing and preparing a 'gay wedding', of whom 12 were found guilty, 11 receiving five-year sentences and one receiving a year; initial reports stated that some were ordered to accept hormone treatments in exchange for lighter sentences. A 2012 raid broke up a party of 30 men in Dubai, and two Indian men arrested that year for consensual sex in a public toilet received six months each plus deportation.

Youth are directly criminalised and vulnerable under the same framework. Residents have no statutory avenue to challenge discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sex characteristics, and no pathway exists to have a legal gender marker corrected.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources describe the 2022 federal code's ceiling on consensual same-sex relations inconsistently: one gives six months as a maximum, while another states a minimum of six months with no maximum prescribed under Article 409(1)(b). The operative sentencing range is unresolved on this inventory.

Whether the 2025 border screening of two trans women produced any formal charge, review or remedy is not sourced here. The Brazilian detainee's allegation of consular negligence is an accusation reported in the press and has not been adjudicated in any material available to this record.

The enforcement reach of Article 412(2) beyond men entering women-only spaces, and whether comparable penalties are applied to trans women whose documents or appearance are read as nonconforming at entry, is not stated in the sources; the border practice is evidenced by traveller accounts rather than by a published screening policy.

Severe restrictions on sex reassignment surgery are described without the operative legal instrument or approval pathway. The absence of documented conversion-practice cases should not be read as evidence of a prohibition, since no law or regulation discourages the practice.
